name: Latest survey window (last year)
plain: The last year of the five-year Census Bureau survey window behind the housing and household figures. A value of 2024 means the figures describe 2020 to 2024.
definition: The year in which the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year window ends. ACS 5-year estimates combine survey responses collected over five calendar years, so 2024 means the window 2020-2024. Every ACS-based field in the municipality record (home values, rents, income, vacancy, cost burden, poverty, employment, education and age) describes that window. All 78 municipalities carry the same value.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. The Census Bureau publishes a new 5-year window each year. In the 2026-10 snapshot the Housing page expects the 2021-2025 window in December 2026.

method: Set once for the whole municipality file (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) and copied into each municipality's record. The comparison window is set the same way (2012, meaning the 2008-2012 window) and is used only by the change fields. Both years are also written to meta.json under housing (acs_latest and acs_base).

values.2024: The ACS 5-year window 2020-2024. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is the only value present (78 of 78 municipalities).

source_detail: US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 window (the 2024 release)
how_to_read: Cite the window, not the single year: write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. A window is built from five years of responses. It is not a count taken on one date.
caveats: The map and the municipality file take the window from a setting that changes only when the observatory is rebuilt. The Housing page series looks for the newest window the Census Bureau has published. After a new window is published, the Housing page can therefore show a newer window than the map and the municipality file until the observatory is rebuilt.
Windows that end one year apart share four of their five survey years, so they are not independent. The 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows share none.

name: Median home value
plain: The middle value among owner-occupied homes in the municipality, as the owners estimate it. Half of these homes are valued above this amount and half below.
definition: Median of the owners' own estimate of what their home would sell for, across all owner-occupied housing units. It is table B25077 ('Median value (dollars)') of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of the window (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory applies no inflation adjustment: the Housing page's 'each survey period's dollars, not adjusted for inflation' means the same, with no conversion between windows.
unit: US dollars of the latest window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B25077, cell 001, for each of the 78 municipalities. The observatory reads the Census Bureau's table-based summary file for the latest window (acsdt5y2024-b25077.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot) and keeps the rows for Puerto Rico's municipalities. The same table for the 2008-2012 window feeds home_value_change_pct.
source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B25077 (median value, owner-occupied housing units); file acsdt5y2024-b25077.dat
how_to_read: A higher amount means owners put a higher price on their homes. It is an opinion of value, not a sale price, and it covers homes people already own, not homes for sale now.
caveats: Owners estimate the value themselves. It is not an appraisal, an assessed value or a recorded sale price.
Only owner-occupied homes are counted. Rented and vacant homes are left out.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±$1,926 (Carolina) to ±$44,042 (Vieques). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

The 2008-2012 value is in the dollars of 2012, not in the dollars of this field, so do not subtract one from the other as if the dollars were the same. 'Change in median home value since 2008-2012 (%)' compares them as published, so it includes general price rises.

plain: The share of renter households that pay 30% or more of their income for rent and utilities. Renter households whose share cannot be worked out are left out. In the 2026-10 snapshot they are about 4 in 10 across the 78 municipalities, so the figure describes the other 6 in 10.
definition: Renter households whose gross rent is 30% or more of household income, divided by renter households for which that share can be computed, times 100. From table B25070 (gross rent as a percentage of household income) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The burdened classes are '30.0 to 34.9', '35.0 to 39.9', '40.0 to 49.9' and '50.0 percent or more'.
unit: % of renter households with a computed rent-to-income share

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

method: B25070 cells 007 to 010 added, divided by (cell 001 minus cell 011 'Not computed'), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b25070.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).

name: Maximum affordable 30-year loan
plain: This is the largest 30-year home loan that a household with the municipality's median income could carry. Three assumptions apply. Housing takes 30% of income. About 78% of that budget (23.5% of income) pays the loan. The interest rate is a fixed 5%. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
definition: A calculation on the median household income of the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Housing may take 30% of income. 78% of that housing budget goes to principal and interest, the part of a mortgage payment that repays the loan and pays the lender (the study's own proportion: $430 of $549). The result is the loan that this monthly payment repays over 30 years at a fixed 5% yearly interest rate. The loan is in the same dollars as the income: the dollars of the window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). It follows the method of Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF) of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023.
unit: US dollars (loan amount), in the dollars of the latest window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

method: monthly housing budget = median household income × 0.30 ÷ 12. Monthly principal and interest = budget × 430/549 (about 0.7832). With r = 0.05 ÷ 12, loan = payment × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. In short, the loan is about 3.65 times median household income. The rate (5%) and the principal-and-interest share (430/549) are fixed settings of the observatory's build. The 30% income share and the 360-month term are written into the calculation itself.
source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B19013; FPR (2023), Table 6 method (Table 8 in the study PDF)
how_to_read: A higher amount means a typical household in the municipality could borrow more under these assumptions. Compare it with the median home value through the affordability ratio. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory; calculated from US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19013, with the affordability method of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023).'
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share (430 of 549) and the 30-year term follow the study's Table 6 method. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. None of these is a lender's rule. Real rates and lending rules differ.
The calculation leaves out the down payment, closing costs, credit history and any other debt.
It uses the median income of all households, renters and owners alike, not of people who plan to buy.
The method gives $80,127 for the study's Puerto Rico median income of $21,967. The study prints $80,181, a gap of $54.
No margin of error is calculated for this field. It inherits the survey margin of the income it is based on.
An illustration of one set of assumptions across municipalities. It is not financial or lending advice and not an estimate of what any household can borrow.
example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Las Marías ($59,507); highest Guaynabo ($170,456). Worked example, Guaynabo: $46,731 income gives a budget of about $1,168 a month, about $915 of it for principal and interest, and a loan of $170,456.

name: Home ownership affordability ratio
plain: The median home value divided by the largest loan a median-income household could carry. Above 1.00, the typical home costs more than the typical household can borrow under the assumptions of the Table 6 method.
definition: median_home_value (table B25077 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) divided by max_affordable_loan, from the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The loan comes from the Table 6 method (Table 8 in the study PDF) of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023. The ratio has no unit: it says how many times the median home value exceeds the maximum affordable loan.
unit: ratio (home value divided by maximum loan)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

method: median_home_value divided by max_affordable_loan, rounded to two decimals. The Housing page profile labels a ratio above 1.00 'out of reach' and a ratio of 1.00 or less 'within reach'. name: Affordability method: settings and rounding rules for the municipality fields
plain: The observatory uses the affordability method of the 2023 housing study by Foundation for Puerto Rico (Table 6 on the Housing page and in this dictionary; Table 8 in the study PDF). It turns median income into the largest 30-year loan a household could carry, then compares that loan with the median home value. This entry lists the settings. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds the method's settings, not coded values.
definition: A four-step calculation. The method comes from The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023 (Table 6 here; Table 8 in the study PDF). (1) Take the median household income of the window (table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates). (2) A household may spend 30% of its income on housing, so the monthly housing budget is income × 0.30 ÷ 12. (3) Of that budget, 430/549 (about 78.3%) goes to principal and interest, the part of the payment that repays the loan and pays the lender. (4) The maximum loan is the amount that this payment repays in full over 360 monthly payments at a fixed 5% yearly rate. The affordability ratio is median home value divided by that loan.

coverage.frequency: Recalculated with each snapshot. The rate stays fixed at 5% in every window.

method: With r = 0.05 ÷ 12: loan = income × 0.30 ÷ 12 × (430/549) × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. Multiplier: about 3.6476 × income. Ratio = median_home_value ÷ loan, rounded to two decimals. The Housing page series uses the same formula for every year. Check against the study: income $21,967 gives $80,127; the study prints $80,181 for Puerto Rico (a gap of $54).

values.30%: Share of income that housing may take.
values.430/549: Share of the housing budget that goes to principal and interest (about 78.3%), the study's own proportion ($430 of $549).
values.5%: Fixed yearly interest rate, the one the study states. Held at 5% in every window and municipality.
values.ratio above 1.00: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs more than the maximum loan: 'out of reach' in the Housing page profile, a warning color on the map's Municipality tab.
values.ratio of 1.00 or less: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs no more than the maximum loan: 'within reach' in the Housing page profile, green on the map's Municipality tab. Because the test uses the rounded ratio, a home that costs slightly more than the maximum loan can still show 1.00 and count as 'within reach'. In the 2026-10 snapshot this is the case for Guayanilla: its median home ($87,400) is $168 above its maximum loan ($87,232), and the ratio rounds to 1.00.

source_detail: FPR (2023), The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF); ACS 5-year tables B19013 and B25077
how_to_read: Use the ratio to compare municipalities with each other under one set of assumptions. Do not use it to say whether a particular family can buy a particular home. Worked example from the 2026-10 snapshot (Guaynabo, 2020-2024 window): median household income $46,731 gives a housing budget of about $1,168 a month, about $915 of it for principal and interest, and a maximum loan of $170,456. The median home value is $226,800, so the ratio is 1.33.
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share ($430 of $549) and the 30-year term are the study's. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. The Housing page notes that actual mortgage rates ranged from under 4% to over 7% over the period it covers.
The method has no down payment, closing costs, credit score or other debt.

Table numbers: this dictionary and the Housing page call the study's affordability table Table 6. The study PDF prints it as Table 8. See 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023): figures and tables on the Housing page'.
Calculated by the observatory from public Census Bureau data. The Census Bureau does not publish it, and no margin of error is calculated for it.

name: How the changes since 2008-2012 are calculated
plain: Each change field compares the latest five-year survey window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) with the 2008-2012 window for the same municipality. Dollar changes are not adjusted for inflation. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds field names, not coded values.
definition: Percent changes are (latest minus baseline) divided by baseline, times 100, rounded to one decimal. The education change is the latest share minus the baseline share, in percentage points. The two windows share no survey years. The baseline is the 2008-2012 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year release, a fixed comparison window of the observatory, read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico sequence files. The latest window is read from the table-based summary files (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

method: The observatory reads the two windows separately and calculates each change from the two medians or shares. The comparison is nominal: the observatory makes no conversion between windows. The Census Bureau reports each window's dollars in its last year (2012 for the baseline; 2024 for the latest window in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2008-2012 income table is titled 'in 2012 inflation-adjusted dollars'; the 2012 titles for home value and rent say only '(DOLLARS)'. The Housing page computes the same kind of change for a base year you choose and says it is not adjusted for inflation.

values.home_value_change_pct: Median home value, table B25077 cell 001, percent change.
values.gross_rent_change_pct: Median gross rent, table B25064 cell 001, percent change.
values.income_change_pct: Median household income, table B19013 cell 001, percent change.
values.bachelors_change_pts: Adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree or higher: B15003 (latest window) minus B15002 (2008-2012), percentage points.
values.population_change_2012_pct: Total population, table B01003 cell 001, percent change.

source_detail: ACS 5-year summary files for the 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows; method modeled on the 2023 study, which compares 2012 with 2021
how_to_read: Read a change as 'higher or lower than in 2008-2012', not as a measured yearly trend. Remember that prices in general rose between the two windows.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.
Only two points in time are compared. What happened between them, such as hurricanes and population loss, is not shown by these fields; the Housing page series has every window.
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are survey estimates.

name: Census tables and cells behind each housing and household field
plain: Use this list to find the Census Bureau table and cell behind each housing and household field. It helps you cite the original numbers. The 'Code' column lists field names in municipalities.json, not coded values.
definition: For each field, the American Community Survey (ACS) table number, the cell numbers used and the calculation. Table numbers are the Census Bureau's own (for example B25077). 'Cell 001' is the first line of the table. In the 2026-10 snapshot the latest window is 2020-2024. The baseline window for the change fields is 2008-2012. In the table-based files the estimate for cell 001 is the column B25077_E001 and its margin of error is B25077_M001.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. The Census Bureau publishes a new 5-year window each year.

method: Latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot): the Census Bureau's table-based summary files, one file per table (acsdt5y2024-<table>.dat), filtered to the rows for Puerto Rico's municipalities (the Census Bureau calls them municipios; geographic codes starting 0500000US72). Baseline window: the 2012 ACS 5-year Puerto Rico sequence files (PuertoRico_All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups.zip), with cells located through the Census Bureau's sequence-and-table lookup file. Tables read for the latest window: B25077, B25064, B19013, B25002, B25004, B25003, B15003, B25070, B25091, B01003, B17001, B01002, B23025. Tables read for the baseline: B25077, B25064, B19013, B15002, B01003.

values.acs_year: Not an ACS cell. The last year of the latest window, set when the observatory is rebuilt (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
values.median_home_value: B25077 cell 001 (median value, owner-occupied housing units). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.median_gross_rent: B25064 cell 001 (median gross rent, renter-occupied units paying cash rent). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.median_hh_income: B19013 cell 001 (median household income in the past 12 months, households). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.seasonal_units: B25004 cell 006 (vacant: for seasonal, recreational, or occasional use).
values.seasonal_pct: B25004 cell 006 divided by B25002 cell 001.
values.owner_occupied_pct: B25003 cell 002 (owner occupied) divided by cell 001 (occupied housing units).
values.renter_cost_burden_pct: B25070 cells 007 to 010 (30.0 percent or more) divided by cell 001 minus cell 011 (not computed).
values.owner_cost_burden_pct: B25091 cells 008 to 011 (30.0 percent or more, with a mortgage) divided by cell 002 minus cell 012 (not computed).
values.poverty_pct: B17001 cell 002 (below the poverty level) divided by cell 001 (population for whom poverty status is determined).
values.employment_rate_pct: B23025 cell 004 (employed civilians) divided by cell 001 (population 16 and over).
values.bachelors_pct: B15003 cells 022 to 025 (bachelor's, master's, professional, doctorate) divided by cell 001 (population 25 and over). Baseline for the change: B15002 cells 015-018 and 032-035 over cell 001.
values.max_affordable_loan: Calculated from B19013 cell 001 with the Table 6 method (see methods.affordability_method).
values.affordability_ratio: Calculated: B25077 cell 001 divided by max_affordable_loan.
values.bachelors_change_pts: Share from B15003 (latest window) minus share from B15002 (2008-2012).
values.population_change_2012_pct: B01003 cell 001 (total population), latest window against 2008-2012.
values.residents_per_unit: Not ACS. 2020 census population (POP100) divided by 2020 census housing units (HU100), Census Bureau TIGERweb.

source_detail: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year summary files. Latest window: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-<table>.dat, one file per table (for example acsdt5y2024-b25077.dat). 2008-2012 baseline: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2012/data/5_year_by_state/PuertoRico_All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups.zip, with cells located through https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2012/documentation/5_year/user_tools/Sequence_Number_and_Table_Number_Lookup.txt
how_to_read: To cite a number, give the table, the window and the geography, for example 'US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B25077, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico'. For a change field cite both windows ('2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012') and both tables. For a calculated field cite the input tables and say who calculated it. If you took the number from the observatory's files rather than from the Census Bureau, cite the observatory as well (Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory).
caveats: The keys of the list are field names in municipalities.json, not codes found in the data.
The observatory reads the Census Bureau's summary files directly and needs no data API key.
Census codes for values that are not available (-666666666 and below) become empty fields. In the 2026-10 snapshot, no estimate in the 2020-2024 files used for the 78 municipalities is negative.

name: How reliable the survey-based housing and household fields are
plain: Survey figures are estimates with a margin of error. The municipality file does not show the margins. Take extra care in small municipalities and with small differences.
definition: The American Community Survey (ACS) interviews a sample of households, so every estimate has a margin of error. The Census Bureau publishes it at the 90% confidence level: it is 90% confident that the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the margin. The municipality file carries estimates only. Margins for most fields are in the Housing page series (housing_series.json, 'moe' values, by window).

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. The Census Bureau publishes a new 5-year window each year.

method: Margins are read from the Census Bureau's own margin columns. For shares and sums the observatory computes margins with the Census Bureau's formulas.
source_detail: US Census Bureau ACS 5-year margins of error; Housing page series (housing_series.json)
how_to_read: Check the margin before ranking or comparing. Add and subtract the margin to get a range for each municipality. If the two ranges overlap, the survey may not be able to tell the municipalities apart. For a formal test, use the Census Bureau's formula for the margin of a difference. In the 2026-10 snapshot, margins are widest in the smallest municipalities, such as Culebra, Vieques, Florida and Maricao.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), margins of error in the Housing page series run across the 78 municipalities as follows: median home value ±$1,926 (Carolina) to ±$44,042 (Vieques); median gross rent ±$16 (San Juan) to ±$240 (Culebra); median household income ±$805 (Mayagüez) to ±$7,604 (Culebra); people below poverty ±1.1 points (San Juan) to ±9.5 points (Culebra); employment rate ±0.7 points (San Juan) to ±5.9 points (Culebra and Vieques); cost-burdened renters ±0.7 points (Gurabo) to ±67.9 points (Florida).
The maximum affordable loan, the affordability ratio and the change fields have no margin of error. Their inputs do.

For total population and for the adult population aged 25 and over the Census Bureau sets the survey totals to its own estimates and often publishes no margin. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) that holds for total population in 76 of 78 municipalities and for the adult population in 73 of 78. The observatory does not calculate a share's margin when the Census Bureau publishes none for the total the share is built on, so shares built on those totals show no margin in the Housing page series (for example 'Adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher (%)'). The Population series and the files below the municipality give such a total a margin of zero instead, so their shares keep the margin of the numerator (methods.small_area_estimates). A missing margin does not mean the figure is exact.
Windows that end one year apart share four of five survey years. A difference between neighboring windows mostly reflects one year of new responses. The 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows share none.
A margin covers sampling error only. It does not cover mistakes in answers, such as owners' estimates of home value.
